World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Farmers angered by plans to turn coal mine into lake bigger than Sydney Harbour
World.content:
For generations, Luke Stuckey's family has bred Angus bulls on a farm at Flynn, in Victoria's Latrobe Valley.

The family farm draws its water from the Latrobe River, which originates on the Baw Baw Plateau, near Mt Baw Baw, and flows through the Latrobe Valley and into the Gippsland Lakes.

Mr Stuckey, a third-generation farmer, said over his lifetime, his family had noticed the effects of climate change on the river.

"It's sort of the last 40, 50 years, my dad especially has noticed a lot of changes," he said.

"The river's deteriorating, the vegetation that's along the river is falling in and creating absolute nightmares for us.

"Flooding is getting a lot more common all the time. In the middle of winter we're having flooding dramas."

Beyond environmental flows, the Latrobe River has a unique role in supplying water to local agriculture and the Latrobe Valley's coal-fired power stations.

But as the power stations close, the plants' owners plan to use river water to fill the massive mine voids they leave behind and turn them into lakes.

The plan is contentious with farmers, who want additional water redirected to agriculture.

Jamie Lowe says similar projects have been carried out overseas. (ABC News: Danielle Pope)

Hazelwood first for rehabilitation

The first coal mine slated for rehabilitation is the massive Hazelwood open cut.

Hazelwood, which closed in 2017, is bigger than Sydney Harbour and separated from the town of Morwell by just four lanes of highway.

The neighbouring Yallourn coal mine will follow in 2028, with the last, Loy Yang, to close in 2035.

Hazelwood's owner, French energy giant Engie, wants to fill it with water from the Latrobe River.

It has conducted environmental assessments and determined that a lake is the safest and most efficient way to rehabilitate the mine.

The company is in the process of developing an environmental effects statement (EES) for the plan.

Hazelwood mine will be the first mine to be rehabilitated in Victoria. (ABC News: Robert French)

Engie head of regulation and compliance Jamie Lowe said the company was looking to successful rehabilitation projects across Australia and overseas for guidance.

"While this project is very much novel for Australia, it is not a new concept to fill a pit lake or to fill a pit with water and turn it into a pit lake, and then to access it for public recreation and other uses," Mr Lowe said.

It will be no small feat if the company achieves its plan.

About 637 gigalitres of water would be needed to fill Hazelwood, over a period of 10 to 20 years.

But locals are concerned about the impact filling the mine with water will have on the Latrobe River and associated economies downstream.

River is a lifeline

As well as managing his farm, Mr Stuckey is president of the Latrobe River Irrigators, a group representing about 40 farmers who irrigate their farms with river water.

He said farmers relied on a secure water supply from the river, particularly during drier periods.

The Latrobe River provides a key irrigation source for many farmers. (ABC News: Danielle Pope)

"Irrigation is used to just be able to lengthen our seasons and get better productivity through the tougher times," Mr Stuckey said.

"[It's a] bit of a drought [insurance] policy as well. We can always have a bit of green grass to keep the cattle going."

Mr Stuckey said farmers were worried reduced flows downstream would place further stress on the river if Latrobe water was used to fill coal mines.

"It's just an absolute waste of quality water," he said.

"We all know the entire environment we are heading towards.

"Everyone keeps saying it's going to be drier. When we do get rain, it will be more rain, but when there's longer periods of less rain, it's just silly."

Lakes system under pressure

Victorian government modelling shows the Latrobe River is drying and since 1997, stream flows in the Latrobe Basin have dropped almost 30 per cent.

The government's Latrobe Valley Regional Water Study found that surface water availability in the Latrobe River system had decreased significantly.

Hayley Sestokas says the government should be considering alternative water sources. (ABC News: Danielle Pope)

Environment Victoria local community organiser Hayley Sestokas said the river was already experiencing negative impacts from years of mining use.

"The impact of that amount of flow being taken from our rivers at a time when we really need to be returning environmental flows to buffer the impacts of climate change and salt inundation in the Gippsland Lakes, really could spell a death knell for our Gippsland Lakes, and the economies, the agriculture and the communities that rely on them," Ms Sestokas said.

Environmentalists want the government to consider other options, including using recycled water to fill the mine.

Lake or liability?

In 2011, significant rain led to a sinkhole, collapsing the walls of the Hazelwood mine.

After significant rain in 2011, the walls of the Hazelwood mine collapsed. (Supplied: ABC News )

The event closed the Princes Freeway for about six months and threatened the nearby town of Morwell, highlighting the need to rehabilitate mines effectively.

Rae Mackay is a hydrogeologist and was appointed as the first Latrobe Valley Mine Rehabilitation Commissioner in 2017.

His position was created after the devastating 2014 Hazelwood mine fire to ensure rehabilitation of the mines would be stable.

Rae Mackay was the former Mine Rehabilitation Commissioner. (ABC News: Danielle Pope)

Professor Mackay said filling the mine pits with water was the most viable option.

"The pit lake option makes it possible to actually use the land around the mines, to use the water within the mines productively with a minimum cost of maintenance," he said.

He said that filling the pit with water would prevent a recurrence of the 2011 highway closure.

"The idea of filling the pit with water is to provide a force, if I can put it that way, that holds the pit batters in place against any environmental action, such as a heavy rainfall event," he said.

Looking forward

Engie said the company understood community concerns about its plan and was working to balance the needs of a safe rehabilitation that worked for everyone, including miners, irrigators and the environment.

"There's no question that the EES is taking a lot longer than we want it to and we appreciate the community frustration that the site isn't further progressed and the EES isn't finalised," Mr Lowe said.

The company said it wanted the state government to advance through to the next stage of its EES so open discussions could be had with all stakeholders about the plan for the pit.

World.title: Tourism industry council warns sector at 'tipping point'
World.content:
Queensland's peak tourism industry body has written to both state and commonwealth governments, calling for immediate and coordinated intervention to stabilise the visitor economy as the sector faces a "tipping point".

According to the Queensland Tourism Industry Council (QTIC) many operators are struggling to remain afloat as they grapple with rising operating costs and cancellations, along with the ongoing fuel crisis.

QTIC chief executive Natassia Wheeler said while the Easter long weekend had provided a welcome increase in bookings for some operators, others had experienced "mass cancellations", alongside a downturn in forward bookings.

Natassia Wheeler says the tourism industry needs "cost relief measures". (Supplied)

"We had caravan parks recording over 200 cancellations, upwards of $52,000 in terms of economic impact and loss to business directly," she said.

"That also doesn't take into account the flow on effect of that loss."

According to figures collected by data company Localis, which derives data from sources including Airbnb, Booking.com and Stayz, accommodation occupancy increased across many regions over the holiday period.

Another 'lockdown': Long-term caravanners face fuel crisis Surging diesel costs have caught many travellers off guard, forcing them to camp out, cancel, or push on and wear the hit to their hip pockets.

In the Whitsundays, Localis found occupancy was up 49.99 per cent, while the Sunshine Coast had an increase of 41.84 per cent. Outback Queensland had a rise of 31.49 per cent, and tropical north Queensland went up by 31.32 per cent.

But Ms Wheeler said these positive occupancy rates may not have necessarily translated to sustainable profitability, with many operators absorbing escalating costs from fuel, insurance, energy and labour.

"This is the tipping point for tourism across Queensland and I'm sure for the country," Ms Wheeler said.

"We need to see cost relief measures, support processes, and look after an industry that's dollar impact is a multiplier."

The QTIC has called on the governments to implement a targeted stabilisation package, with key measures including cost relief for tourism businesses and coordinated action on fuel and aviation costs.

The Sunshine Coast is one of Queensland's most popular tourism destinations. (ABC News: Tara Cassidy)

It has also called for the establishment of a joint state and commonwealth tourism fuel impact taskforce, and clear national guidance to maintain consumer confidence around pricing and surcharges.

Ms Wheeler said the industry was "not asking for a bail out", but rather "targeted, time limited stabilisation".

Fuel crisis hits tourism bookings, cost increases and anxiety over shortages Tourism businesses say they’re bearing the brunt of surging fuel prices, with some losing thousands to booking cancellations and extra operational costs, while others field back-to-calls from tourists about fuel availability.

"There are measurements the federal and state governments can do to support the industry," she said.

"The cost of doing nothing will be higher than [the cost of] acting now. Our regional businesses just do not have the margins to absorb another shock."

In a statement, Minister for the Environment and Tourism Andrew Powell said the Queensland government was "backing our tourism industry" through targeted investment in events, ecotourism, and unique visitor experiences under its Destination 2045 roadmap.

"We know this national crisis is putting pressure on all Queenslanders, and there is plenty more work to be done, which is why we won't be taking a backward step and continue to push for a national dashboard so Queenslanders can access information about where fuel is in the country."

Temporary shutdown considered

On the Sunshine Coast, quad bike tour operator Charles Marais told the ABC he was considering a temporary shutdown, with operating costs now exceeding any money made over the holiday period.

Charles Marais operates a quad bike tour company on the Sunshine Coast. (ABC News: Tara Cassidy)

Not only does he require petrol for the bikes, but also diesel for the bus that transports tourists on a 30-minute drive from Noosa to his property at Cooran, in the hinterland.

"Easter was definitely down on trade, I'd say about 50 per cent of what we usually do," Mr Marais said.

"It all adds up and it does become concerning. I'm thinking about maybe shutting down for a short period myself because the amount of work that's coming in isn't enough to keep it viable."

Sunshine Coast quad bike tour operator Charles Marais is considering a temporary shutdown. (ABC News: Tara Cassidy)

He said he would like to see government support for the industry, similar to measure introduced during the COVID-19 pandemic.

"We need something to come through. I'm in a little bit more of a fortunate position myself I own things outright; I don't have rentals. But other tourism businesses are going to really suffer — we'll see people closing," Mr Marais said.

Business slowing down 'exponentially'

The whale watching season between May and November is normally the busiest time of year for Hervey Bay cruise operator Ben Duffy.

But with bookings for sunset cruises and day trips down by 70 per cent over Easter, Mr Duffy said he was concerned about the future of his business if travellers continued to cancel their plans.

"We've seen [whale cruise bookings] slow down exponentially due to the uncertainty that's around," he said.

Ben Duffy says bookings for whale watching cruises have slowed down "exponentially". (ABC News: James Taylor)

Fuel and other supply costs have risen by around 50 per cent, which Mr Duffy said would force him to make some tough decisions if the crisis does not abate in the coming months.

"I would like to absorb [the higher costs] … because our main passion is taking out people to enjoy what we do every day," he said.

"It's going to be a hard moment in front of the drawing board to figure out what sort of angle we do approach this season with."

Mr Duffy said he believed the reduction to the fuel excise was not enough to alleviate the impact of the higher prices at the bowser, and called for more support for the tourism industry.

Fuel prices the 'tipping point'

A policy briefing provided by QTIC to state and federal governments warned fuel price escalation was now acting as the tipping point in a decade of cumulative pressure, pushing otherwise viable businesses into distress.

In a statement, a federal government spokesperson said the Albanese government would "continue to take every action we can to shield Australians from the impact of this war."

The spokesperson said that included halving the fuel excise, cracking down on petrol companies price gouging, getting more fuel into the market, and working with international partners to secure Australia's fuel supply.

"The tourism minister is holding regular meetings with tourism industry stakeholders as well as state and territory counterparts, and the government will continue to work with the sector to navigate the weeks and months ahead," the spokesperson said.

World.title: Seller disclosure laws driving unethical behaviour, Qld real estate agents say
World.content:
Queensland's seller disclosure laws are driving a "concerning" rise in unethical behaviour like 'gazumping', the state's peak real estate body says.

Agents say there is growing frustration within the industry over the scheme, which was introduced in August last year to improve transparency in property transactions.

Sellers must provide a disclosure statement — known as a Form 2 — to potential buyers before a contract can be signed, with information including zoning details, land contamination, heritage listings, transport resumption plans and rates and water charges.

Buyers can terminate a contract right up to settlement day, get their entire deposit back, and even claim compensation, if the vendor fails to offer up vital information .

The seller disclosure scheme came into effect on August 1 last year. (ABC News: Kate Ainsworth)

'Buyers aren't reading it'

Brisbane real estate agent Brett Andreassen said the statements were ballooning in size, often exceeding 100 pages for apartments and up to 250 pages for houses.

"There's more and more pages being added to the searches through the solicitors — and the buyers aren't reading it," Mr Andreassen said.

" Important things are disclosed in the paperwork but people are just skimming through. "

"Previously, in the contract, disclosures had to be on one page and it had to be clear as day … now, it's being obfuscated," he said.

He warned that could leave buyers vulnerable to costly surprises after purchase, with easements, fees, Body Corp levies, defects and other issues "easily missed".

"If the buyer signs the contract, they can't come back and say it wasn't disclosed," Mr Andreassen said.

Brisbane real estate agent Brett Andreassen says buyers are 'skimming through' seller disclosure statements that are up to 250 pages long. (ABC News: Alex Brewster)

"You can't feign ignorance."

Mr Andreassen said sellers were also paying for extensive searches, often repeated by buyers' solicitors, creating extra expenses for both parties.

"There's a lot of unnecessary duplication going on," Mr Andreassen said.



Queensland-based conveyancer manager Darren Morris said he had encouraged clients to fill out the document themselves, noting it appeared to add minimal value.

"We do probably around 20 settlements a week … I haven’t yet seen where the statement is of a major benefit to a buyer," Mr Morris said.

"I don’t think that the legislation and the documentation is providing any use to really anyone at all, apart from the people making money out of supplying it, like us."

Mr Morris said the focus should remain on buyer-led searches and due diligence.

Conveyancer manager Darren Morris says he does not believe the Form 2 offers a major benefit to buyers. (ABC News: Stephen Clarke)

'Gazumping' risk increase

Real Estate Institute of Queensland (REIQ) chief executive Antonia Mercorella said complexity and delays in preparing the statement had escalated the risk of 'gazumping'.

The unfair and unethical, but not illegal, practice occurs when a vendor accepts an offer informally but then sells the property to someone else before the contract has been legally signed.

"We have seen perhaps that starting to rear its head a little bit," Ms Mercorella said.

"What we have heard is in some instances, particularly in … a fast-moving market … an offer is verbally accepted … the buyer is then told a contract will be put together, along with the Form 2 … and while that Form 2 is being prepared, a better offer comes along that is accepted."

Queensland's seller disclosure laws were designed to improve transparency, but can lead to delays. (ABC News: Liz Pickering)

"There's an argument that because there's time required to put the Form 2 together … and because there's a delay between that offer being made and the contract being ready … buyers have been 'gazumped,'" she said.

Ms Mercorella described the trend as "concerning" but said it was not "widespread".

"A verbal offer as a general rule is not enforceable … it must be in writing, but nonetheless that's a dreadful situation to be in," Ms Mercorella said.

Antonia Mercorella said the Real Estate Institute of Queensland had written to the attorney-general about the industry's concerns. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

"It's not happening at a large scale but one can see how perhaps that risk has been escalated because of the requirement to prepare the Form 2 … there's an argument it allows people to come out of the woodwork and make another offer that's better."

"That is not the intent of this regime and it shouldn't be used in that way," she said.

Mortgage broker Rebecca Jarrett-Dalton said the increase was worrying but expected, and said gazumping was common in competitive property markets.

She said it could be distressing and expensive, particularly for first-home buyers.

Mortgage broker Rebecca Jarrett-Dalton says gazumping can be common in competitive property markets. (Supplied)

"They don't know the law, they're very new at the whole process," Ms Dalton said.

"It's a really tricky market for them as is so it becomes really disheartening."

She urged prospective buyers to consult with their solicitor and broker throughout the entire process and to be as familiar with all documents and contracts as possible.

State government reviewing scheme

Brisbane agent Gabrielle Trickey said there was also ongoing confusion about what must be included in the statement, with key issues — like natural hazard history and asbestos presence — not covered.

She said a property's flood history should be disclosed, arguing it was critical information.

"Without it, it doesn't pass the pub test — we should not be 'pussyfooting' around that," Ms Trickey said.

" You shouldn't have any buyer walking blindly into purchasing a house or unit that's been flooded. "

Both agents called for the laws to be refined and simplified, arguing the current regime risks overwhelming buyers rather than informing them.

Ms Mercorella said the REIQ wrote to the Attorney-General Deb Frecklington late last year to outline the industry's concerns.

Real estate agent Gabrielle Trickey wants to see the seller disclosure laws refined and simplified. (ABC News)

"The Attorney-General committed to a review [and] we're quietly optimistic that through that … we can improve the document and improve the process," she said.

A spokesperson for Ms Frecklington said the government continued to "closely monitor" the scheme with input from industry stakeholders and a working group, comprising of various relevant bodies including the REIQ.

"Seller disclosure laws are designed to clarify legal obligations for both parties through a more transparent sale process and result in fewer post-contractual disputes, bringing Queensland into line with other states," the spokesperson said.

World.title: Tourists urged not to cancel plans as Cyclone Maila nears Far North Qld
World.content:
The Bureau of Meteorology says the impacts of Severe Tropical Cyclone Maila, which is looming about 1,300 kilometres off Queensland, will be largely confined to the Far North.

The category three cyclone is expected to cross Cape York Pennisula on Sunday afternoon, bringing strong winds and heavy rainfall.

But senior forecaster Liam Smart said Maila would not be as intense as ex-Tropical Cyclone Narelle, which reached category five before battering the Cape York Peninsula last month.

"[They're] two quite different cyclones," he said.

"Maila is a lot bigger than Narelle and probably not going to be as strong."

Tourism operators who lost bookings due to Narelle are urging visitors not to cancel their plans.

Intensity changing as cyclone moves

On Wednesday morning, Maila was about 980km east of Port Moresby, in Papua New Guinea, with wind gusts of up to 295km/h.

It could intensify as it moves slowly over the Solomon Sea before tracking south-west by Thursday.

Mr Smart said Maila may lose intensity as it moves west over PNG's mountain ranges and into the cooler Coral Sea.

Ex-Tropical Cyclone Narelle made landfall in March. (ABC News)

"There's a bit of uncertainty as to where the cyclone will cross," he said.

"We're expecting somewhere between, say, Cooktown and the tip of the peninsula, but as the time gets a little bit closer we'll be able to pinpoint that location more."

Mr Smart said rainfall associated with Maila should "be relatively confined to the Far North area".

"But there is potential for some extra rainfall as some easterly winds start pushing on the coast after the cyclone has crossed into potentially the north tropical coast area," he said.

Severe weather turns tourists away

Hundreds of kilometres south of where Cyclone Maila is forecast to make landfall, Port Douglas tourism operator Jason Heffernan is asking visitors not to abandon their travel plans.

He said the biggest challenge during cyclone warnings was misinformation or misunderstandings about Queensland's size.

Jason Heffernan says tourists should proceed with their plans despite the cyclone. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

"A lot of people down south think that as soon as you see a cyclone in the Coral Sea, Cairns and Port Douglas are being hit," Mr Heffernan said.

"But in reality it's the same distance as Melbourne to Canberra."

Port Douglas experienced heavy rain and strong winds during Narelle last month, but Mr Heffernan said many tourists unnecessarily cancelled their trips after those conditions subsided.

"We definitely do see people nervous, wanting to cancel their entire holiday plans, and generally it's just not required," he said.

"The rainforest needs the rain, and so if you come here after the wet or just on the wet, the rainforest is going to be green.

"I just hope that people maybe saw that the last cyclone, Narelle — which this one seems to be following almost a similar path — didn't affect us at all."

More cyclones than average

The tropical cyclone season runs from November to the end of April.

BOM senior climatologist Zhi-Weng Chua said there had been 10 tropical cyclones in the Australian region this season, six of which reached category three or higher.

"The average number of cyclones that make landfall is three to four and we've had six so far," he said.

Cyclone Maila is expected to be the seventh cyclone to make landfall in Australia this season. (Supplied: Bureau of Meteorology)

Maila will be the seventh severe tropical cyclone to make landfall should it cross Far North Queensland this weekend.

"Having 10 tropical cyclones so far and likely to have 11, that would be tracking at least slightly above average," Mr Chua said.

The weather outlook for the rest of Queensland will be settled and mostly sunny this week, with some isolated showers north of Mackay on Wednesday.

Some showers are also expected north of Gladstone in Central Queensland on Thursday, with scattered showers between Ingham and Cooktown in the Far North.

Above-average temperatures are forecast for central and southern Queensland.

World.title: Police 'recommence' reporting of child abuse by staff after eight-month gap
World.content:
Tasmania's child safety regulator has addressed an "untenable situation" where police officers may have been exempt from a key measure to safeguard children from abuse.

The Office of the Independent Regulator (OIR) oversees organisations' compliance with mandatory reporting for suspected or confirmed child abuse involving staff.

In Tasmania, organisation heads are required to report to the OIR, triggering an investigation and an update to the regulator within 30 days.

Tasmania Police stopped complying in August last year, the regulator said.

The regulator is concerned there may be an eight-month gap in mandatory reporting. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

It said Tasmania Police advised that it had legal advice that mandatory reporting did not apply to police officers.

"To remedy this untenable situation, the OIR has met with the Attorney-General and has put forward a regulatory amendment to explicitly include Tasmania Police, ideally retroactively from 1 August, 2025," the regulator said.

Serious police officer misconduct allegations increase in Tasmania Allegations of the most serious rated police misconduct have more than doubled in three years, according to police data.

The state government said this "urgent fix" took effect last week, but it was not yet able to confirm if Tasmania Police would be required to account for the eight-month gap in reporting.

Independent Regulator Louise Coe told state parliament she requested the change be made retrospectively.

"Because from 1 August last year they had stopped reporting the identity of matters through to my office," she said.

"I know there have been instances [in that time period] where there's been significant interactions with young people I'm concerned about," Ms Coe said.

Independent Regulator Louise Coe told parliament about her concerns. (Supplied: OIR)

Ms Coe said the legal advice police provided said it could not give the names of police officers involved to the regulator.

"With our system, we put the subject of [the] allegation's details in … and track that profile, so that [omission] is a concerning aspect," she told parliament.

Tasmania Police told the ABC it wrote to the regulator because it had been reviewing its procedures under state child safety legislation.

Police to internally review matters, parliament hears

Ms Coe's comments were made during a parliamentary hearing for the recommendations of Tasmania's commission of inquiry into child sexual abuse.

Greens call for parliamentary inquiry into paedophile cop Paul Reynolds The Greens will push for Tasmania's parliament to scrutinise how police handled child abuse allegations against former officer Paul Reynolds, and why it was decided to give him a full police funeral.

The commission's recommendations led to law changes in 2024 in relation to mandatory reporting.

Tasmania Police was among organisations scrutinised in the state's commission of inquiry, which found the police force did not adequately respond to "credible reports" emerging about the late paedophile cop Paul Reynolds, who groomed and sexually abused up to 52 children.

Greens MLC Cassy O'Connor asked Ms Coe whether Tasmania Police had informed her whether the organisation had "any sort of child safety framework of policies or practices in place ... given there's been a history of the most egregious breaches of trust and damage to children".

Upper house Greens MLC Cassy O'Connor questioned the independent regulator in parliament. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Ms Coe replied: "Up until that sort of change in focus, I think there's been quite good engagement [with Tasmania Police]", which she said had implemented a child safety action plan.

"It's just really concerning now that it's a gap," Ms Coe said.

"We've seen some matters that have come through reception prisons involving police officers. That's concerning. And we don't have oversight of that," she said.

In Tasmania, children accused of crime can be held in adult reception prisons in watch houses — something advocates have long called for an end to.

Ms Coe said told parliament she had heard of "some matters" at Tasmania's reception prisons. (Supplied: The Office of the Custodial Inspector's Children in Tasmania's prisons review report 2025)

"And what happens in that instance if a young person reports they've been physically or sexually harmed by a Tasmanian Police employee?" Ms O'Connor then asked.

"My understanding is they [Tasmania Police] will still do an internal review," Ms Coe said.

Tasmania Police 'updating protocols'

When the ABC asked Tasmania Police if it wrote to the regulator about its legal advice and why it did so, it did not directly answer but pointed to the resulting legislative changes, saying it would "recommence referrals under the Reportable Conduct Scheme" from April 1.

"Tasmania Police is committed to being a child safe organisation and this includes having the reporting and oversight procedures in place to appropriately respond to any suspicion of harm to a child or young person," it said.

Tasmania Police said it had been reviewing its procedures when it got legal advice that it was not an "entity" under the mandatory reporting act. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

When the ABC asked its questions again, Tasmania Police said its "legal advice determined Tasmania Police were not an entity for the purposes of the Child and Youth Safe Organisations Act 2023, and, as such, not able to provision certain information to the OIR".

"Tasmania Police had been undertaking a review of its procedures under the act, and developing protocols in relation to disclosure of information for the purpose of the Reportable Conduct Scheme in part 4 of the act".

Sectors with most child safety notifications

Since Australia's Royal Commission into Child Sexual Abuse in 2017, most states have now adopted reportable conduct schemes which obligate leaders of certain organisations to report concerns of child sexual abuse involving a staff member.

The inquiry's final report stated police officers were among a "wide range of organisations" that must comply with mandatory reporting.

Like in the federal royal commission, Tasmanian institutions and the government were found to have failed to properly respond to allegations and incidents of child abuse.

Tasmania's regulator received 567 notifications of potential misconduct in the 2024-25 financial year, an increase from 9 to 12 per week from the year before.

The regulator received notifications of potential misconduct at the Ashley Youth Detention Centre in 2024-25. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Thirty-four of those reports were substantiated, according to the regulator's annual report — with some alleged victims in multiple notifications.

A total of 452 were still open at the end of the reporting year.

A third of total notifications came from the education sector, with 189 notifications made to the regulator.

There were 133 from child protection services and out-of-home care — with data suggesting 16 per cent of children and youth in out-of-home care were alleged victims in a reportable conduct notification.

Meanwhile, data suggested 47 per cent of young people in Ashley Youth Detention Centre were alleged victims in a notification.

World.title: Outback tensions rise as national parks expansion reshapes communities
World.content:
Loading...

It resembles an inland sea — teeming with birdlife.

Deep in the outback, Narriearra-Caryapundy Swamp National Park is probably not what you'd expect to find after a 15-hour drive from Sydney.

The former outback cattle station is located in the north-west corner of New South Wales.

It was the first in a series of properties purchased by the NSW government in recent years.

A black kite glides through the sky. ( )

Its stated goal is to increase conservation and attract tourists.

But the purchases, according to graziers, have had unintended consequences.

They're fed up and are saying enough is enough.

Three hundred and fifty kilometres south of Narriearra-Caryapundy, a herd of black cattle marches into stockyards.

The air is filled with the sound of their bellows as their hard hooves hit the ground amid the roar of mustering motorbikes.

Watching on from the back of a rusted-out truck is grazier Sam Beven.

Alongside him is his heavily pregnant wife, Erin, and their three young boys Harvey, 6, Duncan, 4, and Walter, 2.

But as he watches, questions linger in Sam's mind.

What does the future hold for his children? What if they all want to get into farming? And how will they afford it?

Sam Beven took over the property from his father two years ago. ( )

The Beven boys Harvey (6), Duncan (4) and Walter (2). ( )

Contractors move the cattle into the yards. ( )

Sam and Harvey go for a ride around the property. ( )

For Sam, working the land has always been his dream.

He grew up here at Sturt's Meadows Station, 70 kilometres north of Broken Hill.

The outback property has been his family's home since 1951.

"I love working with sheep, working with cattle. I love animals, always have loved animals," he says.

"Absolutely everything about it is just so appealing to me."

At 33 years old, his dream has become a reality.

Sam hopes one day his boys will be able to follow in his footsteps — but he's not so sure they can.

A view from above the yards at Sturt's Meadows. ( )

In recent years, the daily stresses of agriculture have been increased by what he sees as a looming existential threat.

The NSW government has spent around $200 million acquiring 16 large outback stations since 2020.

The vast and spectacular channel country at Thurloo Downs. ( )

It has added one million hectares to the national park estate for conservation.

It's an area more than four times the size of the ACT.

Sand dunes stretch off into the horizon. ( )

Thurloo Downs, located along the Queensland border, was the most expensive at $108,082,411.

The 437,000-hectare station features rivers, salt lakes, flood plains, sand dunes and woodland areas.

NSW National Parks sees it as a potential jewel in the crown of its western estate.

A sanctuary for threatened species and other fauna and flora, it's expected to become a drawcard for tourists in the coming decades.

But the conversion of Thurloo and more than a dozen other large outback stations is troubling to local landholders.

Many graziers across the vast pastoral area believe these purchases threaten their futures.

The property is almost eight times the size of greater Sydney. ( )

Five staff will be employed to manage the park. ( )

Former environment minister James Griffin at Thurloo Downs for the sale announcement in 2023. ( )

The Bevens run cattle and sheep at their station. ( )

It's something Sam and Erin Beven discuss often.

"What do we do in 10 years, 20 years, 30 years … where are we going to be? What if the kids do this? What if the kids do that?" Sam says.

As more properties are sold, it creates more questions for Sam and many like him.

Rising land values are also of concern.

In 2020, the average rural New South Wales property was worth $673,218.

The latest data from the NSW Valuer General shows it has almost doubled to $1,264,400 in 2025.

Areas in the state's west, including Bourke, Cobar and the Central Darling Shire, have seen average rural land values increase by as much as 138 per cent.

Taking notes as cattle enter the yards. ( )

Rural land values around Cobar rose 138 per cent from July 2020 to July 2025. ( )

Some graziers like Sam Beven believe these prices have been inflated, at least in part, by national park purchases.

"To have the land value skyrocket the way it has is a bit frightening when it comes to … can we expand?" he says.

"We're about to have four kids — what if they all want to take over?

"We can't buy another property somewhere; we can't make this one bigger … how do we deal with this?"

Although their land is likely rising in value, it has downsides for families.

Sam, who is the president of the Pastoralists Association of West Darling, has heard these concerns from many people across the district.

"Everything that we do is so that we can give a better place than we took over to our kids," he says.

" If it's just too expensive for the kids to take on, it's almost like it's for nothing. "

A map of the stations purchased since the middle of 2020. ( )

Sam believes there are alternative arrangements available to the government.

He suggests property owners could set aside land for conservation, especially in areas that are too hard to fence or muster.

"I mean, if there was one paddock on every property tied up for this conservation, it'd probably be more than the land they purchased.

"But everyone can still run their livestock operation, they're just a paddock short."

Bourke was once one of the country's busiest inland ports. ( )

More than 600km away in the remote agricultural town of Bourke, similar questions are being asked.

Known for its quality wool production and a once bustling inland port, graziers here are also worried about what these station sales might mean.

In the past four years, seven former livestock operations around Bourke and nearby Cobar have been bought for about $32 million, accounting for 105,000 hectares of land.

Grazier Richard Ridge has been a vocal advocate against the accelerated expansion of these national parks.

"It's really destroying our social fabric of the Bourke community as well as surrounding communities," he says.

The 34-year-old worries about what will happen when there are fewer pastoral operations that need local supplies, support and workers.

Richard Ridge, his wife Jacqui and their twin boys Hugh and Ed. ( )

"It's just meaning less and less people out in these pastoral zones," he says.

"You want to have more people out here [because] it's a productive area. In good seasons … you can't beat it."

Over the past few years, successive NSW governments have conducted little to no community consultation about these park purchases.

According to graziers and the Bourke Shire Council, it has left an information vacuum.

"Some of us have reached out to people in the department, and we've heard crickets," Richard says.

"It's pretty concerning when you don't know what they're aiming to do and they don't want to talk to you."

There are more than 20 million sheep in NSW. ( )

Mount Gundabooka is roughly 50km from Bourke. ( )

He also doubts the newly created parks will bring a lot more tourists.

"We've got Mount Gundabooka … I have absolutely no problem [with it], it's a beautiful place to go and visit.

"The historic Toorale Station … these are drawcards to your community.

"[But] if you're buying satellite parks all over the shire, I don't see how this is going to bring extra people into Bourke."

'Enough is enough'

Loading...

Richard's father, Phillip, has lived at Jandra Station for more than four decades.

He's concerned about the effect land purchases are going to have on future generations.

Phillip Ridge believes other arrangements are available to increase conservation and maintain farming operations. ( )

"Bourke has been a very prosperous district for 160 years, the largest wool gathering point in the world at one stage," he says.

"It's just starting to get to the point where it's tipping too much in the way of conservation.

"We feel enough is enough."

Phillip says the lack of communication is worrying.

"If that was a corporate business, OK, you'd wear it on the chin, but … this is actually our taxpayers' money.

" It's our taxpayer dollars seen really in an undemocratic way to be devoiding us of our income, our prosperity. "

Phillip and many other graziers support conservation and are not against the National Parks organisation and its locally based staff.

But they question if it's necessary to remove a million hectares of productive land, given the consequences.

"My lifestyle has been a happy one — I want it to be for my children and their children," Phillip says.

Phillip Ridge's cattle dog rides along in the back of the ute. ( )

It's not just farmers who have concerns.

Bourke Shire Deputy Mayor Sally Davis believes the station sales are having a detrimental effect across the region.

Having seen the population drop in Bourke in recent decades, she's worried.

The council doesn't believe the additional economic benefit of these parks will offset the loss of farming operations.

"We will not get enough revenue out of tourism into this shire by people coming out to the national parks," she says.

"Nothing compared to the production that's come off the land by the previous owners."

Sally Davis is worried the newly purchased national parks won't make up for the loss of farming. ( )

The population of the Bourke shire is less than 2,500 people, and being located more than 750km north-west of Sydney, Sally Davis believes their voices aren't being heard.

She believes the state government isn't going to slow down its purchases.

"They are clearly targeting these areas out here because they're bigger expanses of land.

"We don't have the number of voters out here; the voters are obviously on the coastline.

" They're the ones that dictate what happens regardless of their ability to understand what goes on out here. "

Roy Butler wants councils and landholders included in the national park discussions. ( )

Bourke Shire Council and the local independent state member, Roy Butler, have called for a stop to national park purchases by the government until the consultation process is improved.

"Each one of these properties on average contributes about $500,000 to the local economy when it's operating as an agricultural property, so we need to replace that income," Mr Butler says.

"I'm not against national parks at all, I think national parks are really important, but what we're doing is taking a lot of money out of communities and councils and we're not replacing it with the visitor infrastructure that's needed to bring the tourists out."

Both he and the council would also like to see a cost-benefit analysis to determine whose wants and needs take priority: locals concerned about economic change and family legacy, or government claiming to act on behalf of the state, the broader population and the environment.

Jaymie Norris has spent more than a decade working for the NPWS. ( )

On the other side of this story is Jaymie Norris, who works for National Parks.

He's been the Far West area manager for almost a decade, based in Broken Hill.

But Jaymie's roots here run deep.

His family has been in the area for around 150 years, working in mining and agriculture.

He says he understands the impact of farming on rural communities and the concerns graziers have about the new parks.

"The only way for western New South Wales to be successful is to have very healthy mining, tourism and grazing industries.

"In that tourism space, the National Parks [and Wildlife] Service plays a really important, integral role."

Local Indigenous ranger Glen O'Donnell oversees Langidoon-Metford. ( )

Langidoon-Metford National Park is covered with evidence of pre-colonial history. ( )

Langidoon-Metford National Park is 65km east of Broken Hill.

The two properties were purchased five years ago, before being destocked and merged for conservation.

A handful of local rangers and Indigenous people help maintain the park, which, according to Jaymie, is covered with evidence of pre-colonial history.

"Just the road from the highway through to the campground, which is about 9km … there were over 12,000 Aboriginal artefacts," he says.

A variety of items have been found here, including small chips, large grinding dishes, and other gender-based cultural items for ceremony.

"There's a lot of stuff … and when the wind and rain come, just more and more come up … [we're] always finding new ones," says Glen O'Donnell, a local NPWS ranger.

The Darling River at Menindee. ( )

The 16 properties purchased in recent years also have a surprisingly diverse outback landscape.

They encompass the beauty of the Darling River as well as the red rolling hills of the Strzelecki Desert …

The spectacular channel country on offer at Thurloo Downs. ( )

… to the ephemeral lakes and channel country up north near the Queensland border at Thurloo Downs and Narriearra-Caryapundy …

… as well as vast woodlands of Langidoon-Metford and the sacred sites and Indigenous rock art at Mutawintji National Park.

New and old Aboriginal hand stencil art at Mutawintji National Park. ( )

"For someone travelling from the city, you feel like you're in a different country," Jaymie says.

"The national parks give you the opportunity to go out and engage throughout that landscape like you can't anywhere else."

Tourism and the environment

Hundreds of thousands of visitors travel through western NSW every year.

Beyond conservation, Jaymie believes the land purchases will only continue to increase tourism, as more infrastructure is built and roads are improved.

"About 250,000 people stay per annum in terms of overnight accommodation, whether that's camping or with hard-roof accommodation," he says.

National Parks estimates these visitors, alongside investment in the parks, contribute around $400 million to the region each year.

Thousands of tourists travel through Bourke each year. ( )

Broken Hill is the closest centre to many of the newly purchased national parks. ( )

But beyond this, he says removing stock from the land benefits the environment.

"The vast majority of conservation outcomes are actually driven by graziers," Jaymie says.

"National Parks only manages a very small proportion of the landscape — areas where conservation is the primary focus, where you're able … to remove that grazing pressure, particularly from hard-hoofed animals.

"You can derive great environmental benefit that can't be achieved through the continued practice of grazing."

Hard-hooved animals like sheep can impact native flora. ( )

Sam Beven employs contractors to help muster cattle. ( )

There's always a straggler ... ( )

National implications

The tension between graziers and the NSW government may seem like a local issue, but there's also international pressure.

The federal government has signed up to the United Nations Kunming-Montreal protocol, which sets a target for 30 per cent of Australia's land and marine areas to be managed for conservation by 2030.

According to Jaymie Norris, New South Wales is lagging well behind that goal.

It's also one of the reasons landholders are concerned that many more large outback stations will continue to be purchased, further reducing grazing communities.

"NSW has the second-least amount of land that is conserved within a conservation estate at about 11 per cent," Jaymie says.

Some states like South Australia and Western Australia are already around the 30 per cent mark, he adds.

Alex Graham says the new purchases capture unique landscapes. ( )

Alex Graham was appointed as the boss of NSW National Parks less than a year ago.

She says the new purchases capture unique landscapes that are under-represented in the parks estate.

"We don't have a set target by hectares or percentage," she says.

Alex Graham looks out at the Darling River at Menindee. ( )

"What we do have is an establishment plan, which guides our strategic decision-making around acquisitions."

National Parks is in the process of updating the plan, with consultation scheduled for this year.

The sale of Tasman and Corinya stations to National Parks was announced in December. ( )

When the rural business of a station finishes, work for shearers and other contractors stops.

But National Parks has had to create jobs after acquiring so many properties in recent years.

A black monitor lizard at Tasman Station. ( )

It now employs about 300 people across the state's west.

"Over a third of our staff, for example in western New South Wales, are ex-pastoralists," Ms Graham says.

More than 50 per cent of National Parks staff are Indigenous.

"This means that we've got really fantastic knowledge and expertise of the land management that's right for the area," she says.

Ms Graham disagrees that the loss of these farming operations will have anywhere near as big an impact as is being claimed by landholders and councils.

"National Parks also require all of those services that private properties require in terms of land management," she says.

"We have infrastructure, we have housing, we have roads to maintain, and we require staff and contractors."

She argues inflation and commodity prices have helped increase the cost of rural land, not just successive Labor and Coalition governments with plenty of money to spend.

Claims that the government is outcompeting pastoral families for stations is incorrect, she says.

"We've purchased around 15 properties in the last five years. Last year there were 45 properties on the market that were greater than 2,000 hectares — we purchased one of those.

"But I do hear their concerns and appreciate that there is a lot of pressure there for local communities, particularly in getting into the market."

Loading...

Alex Graham says inflation and commodity prices have helped increase the cost of rural land. ( )

National Parks says its total expenditure in western NSW was $87 million in 2024-25. ( )

But Ms Graham won't rule out future purchases.

"Where we see properties that come onto the market that offer opportunities for … protections for those under-represented values, then we will consider those."

She concedes communication needs to improve with local councils and graziers.

"It's very much about listening and partnering and doing this together.

"If we can give them more information about what we're doing in terms of land management, then they're more empowered to partner with us and offer us suggestions on the sorts of things that they would like to see us do."

Back out at Sturt's Meadows north of Broken Hill, Sam Beven, Erin, and their three boys watch the sun disappear behind the distant ranges.

Always in the back of Sam's mind is his family's future.

The 16 station acquisitions have no doubt introduced added anxiety to his life and that of many other graziers.

This is despite the best intentions of the state government to improve conservation and tourism.

He says it's made the everyday challenges of agriculture that little bit harder.

The family watching the sunset together. ( )

Boys being boys. ( )

Sam Beven playing with his son Walter. ( )

Not knowing what the government and National Parks have planned for future purchases also adds another layer of stress.

But regardless of the uncertainty, there remains one sure thing for the Beven family.

They want their future to be here, surrounded by red earth.

"There's the whole family atmosphere that we've built here, for generations we've been working on this," Sam says.

" I would be absolutely devastated if a place like this was no more because it became a national park. "

The Beven family — Erin, Duncan, Harvey, Walter and Sam. ( )

NSW Environment Minister Penny Sharpe says she wants to work with local councils and communities to maximise the number of people who visit the region's national parks.

"Western NSW contains some of the least protected environments in the country," she told the ABC in a statement.

"Each new acquisition helps protect these fragile places and extraordinary Aboriginal cultural heritage, while bringing new life into regional towns through new tourism opportunities and government investment."

Her spokesperson told the ABC the minister deferred to National Parks to speak about the new parks and the station purchases.

World.title: Matt Canavan looks to stars for 'Australia on steroids' plan
World.content:
A domestic space industry, a baby boom, new dams and more factories are on Nationals leader Matt Canavan's to-do list to deliver what he describes as an Australian economic revolution.

The vision for "an Australia on steroids" will be set out by Senator Canavan during his first major address since winning the Nationals leadership last month.

Speaking at the National Press Club, Senator Canavan will lay out a five-point plan to revive the economy.

"I am proposing an Australian economic revolution, not a replay or a reset," Senator Canavan will tell the press club, according to a draft speech seen by the ABC.

He has dubbed the plan a Patriot Agenda for an Australian Economic Revival.

"We won't get revival by tinkering around the edges. Some of this will require the long-overdue slaying of sacred cows.

"The first sacred cow that must go is our naive belief that open borders for goods and people are always and everywhere a good thing."

The fight for 126,000 square kilometres of Coalition heartland The upcoming Farrer by-election is already being talked about as a litmus test for the new opposition leader and an ascendant One Nation. It'll also be a measure of major party politics.

Current border settings have not been working, leaving the door open to tariffs to protect Australian industries, he will say.

Senator Canavan will argue for a national works program to build infrastructure projects like dams and roads, as well as both seaports and spaceports.

"Our continent is uniquely placed for rocket launches," he will say, pointing to the Australian Space Agency, previously established by the Coalition.

Not only could a renewed space age help secure Australia communications, defence and national security interests, it could also boost regional populations, according to the Nationals leader.

Senator Canavan's ambitious plan would require a significant shift in fortunes for the Coalition, which was significantly weakened following last year's federal election.

Restoring manufacturing and fuel security

Senator Canavan will identify the steel industry as a sector worth protecting, which he will say has fallen victim to overseas imports.

"Australia is the largest exporter of coking coal and iron ore in the world, the two main ingredients to make steel," he said.

"We should not need to import foreign steel but, just like on fuel, we have become reliant on other countries for a basic material because we have not acted in response to their protective barriers."

Scrapping the net zero plan, he will say, is key to a successful manufacturing industry and domestic fuel security.

"To restore sovereign capability and unleash energy abundance, we must end net zero, scrap all carbon taxes and end all bans on energy production in Australia," he will tell the press club.

"A real Made in Australia agenda will only work when it is fuelled by all types of Australian energy," he will say, in reference to the Albanese government's multi-billion-dollar push to spur local manufacturing and renewables.

In addition to calling for the borders to be closed to "mass migration", he will argue for measures to boost the birthrate, including favourable tax settings for dual-income households and promoting working from home.

The Nationals leader argues abandoning net zero is essential to supporting Australian manufacturing and industry. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

The measures, he will say, would also help to increase populations in regions and smaller towns.

"In the past the opening of a new mine or factory could convince the whole family to move but today, unless the other partner has a job in their career, the family will likely stay and fly in and out instead," he will tell the press club.

Promoting working from home in professional jobs and in the public services would help to make regional relocations a possibility for families, according to his speech.

"The public service should lead by example, and we should look at tax incentives or infrastructure concessions to encourage it in the private sector too," he will say.

A focus on Farrer

While the Nationals leader's grand vision involves turning his gaze towards the stars, his address also focuses closer to home and specifically towards next month's Farrer by-election.

In promoting the growth of regional centres, Senator Canavan argues for more services in those centres.

He will point to Albury Wodonga Health as an example of where service delivery has failed.

The service has been beset by problems in recent years and its executive management was the subject of a no-confidence vote by doctors last month.

Senator Canavan will argue a plan to grow and develop regional Australia would help to relieve the strain on services in big cities and boost those in country areas.

The Farrer by-election was triggered by Sussan Ley's resignation. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Albury Wodonga Health is shaping up to be a major election issue leading in to the May by-election, along with concern about the Murray Darling and water security for growers.

The Coalition has already announced a commission of inquiry into the Murray Darling, and Senator Canavan will argue dam building and refurbishment are required to protect the foodbowl.

"If we don't start planning now for their refurbishment we will lose our nation's food bowl," he will say.

World.title: Oil shock hits 'at worst possible time' for quake-stricken, war-racked country
World.content:
A monastery sheltering about 100 people in northern Myanmar has been bombed by the military, killing monks and civilians in what rights groups say is part of a broader pattern of attacks on religious sites.

The air strike on March 20 hit the monastery in Katha, in Sagaing region — a town where author George Orwell once lived and which inspired his novel Burmese Days.

A year ago, a devastating 7.7-magnitude earthquake centred on the Sagaing region killed thousands of people and destroyed homes and infrastructure across six regions and states.

The effects are still being felt, with attempts to rebuild hindered by the junta's continued attacks on civilian infrastructure — including religious buildings.

"Monasteries are where people come together to eat, to pray, to survive," said Thinzar Shunlei Yi, a pro-democracy activist who founded the NGO Sisters 2 Sisters, which provides aid to women.

"The military is now attacking the heart of our faith: the Buddhist monkhood and our religious spaces," she told the ABC.

She said the military appeared to be targeting areas it believed were linked to resistance forces, including monasteries, treating those sheltering there as enemies.

"They are indiscriminately attacking all civilians … even religious sites supporting community members as a shelter," Thinzar Shunlei Yi explained, after speaking to survivors.

She added that the attacks appear aimed at instilling fear and tightening control as junta leader Min Aung Hlaing was elected as president in an election widely seen by Western governments as a "sham".

A monastery compound in Katha after Myanmar military air strikes. (Supplied: People's Defence Force/DVB)

The strike in Katha was not an isolated incident.

A day later, a monastery and school in Kani township, east of Mandalay, were bombed, according to local news reports.

This week in Karen State, along the border with Thailand, another monastery was reportedly attacked.

Since the military seized power from Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government in February 2021 in a coup, peaceful demonstrations were put down with lethal force, and many opponents of the military rule took up arms.

Young monks help clear rubble in rebuilding efforts. (AFP: Sai Aung Main)

Thinzar Shunlei Yi said these recent attacks in Sagaing region, which is a stronghold of armed resistance against the military, showed there was nowhere safe for civilians.

"Once they bomb monasteries — places that support the community — it's an attack on people's mindset, the mindset of resistance," she said.

The military did not reply to a request for comment.

Rights groups, including Karen Human Rights Group, have documented the Myanmar military's attacks on religious buildings as part of its widespread, post-coup campaign against civilians.

Aid blocked — including menstrual pads

Aid groups say blockades in Sagaing region are ongoing, with the Myanmar military continuing to restrict the flow of basic supplies into areas hit by conflict and the earthquake.

"They intentionally put in a policy to block the delivery of menstrual products," said Thinzar Shunlei Yi.

Grassroots groups, including Sisters 2 Sisters, are still trying to raise funds and deliver gender-specific aid — sanitary pads and medical supplies — to women in affected areas.

Their volunteers were recently blocked from distributing aid in Pale and Yin Mar Pin in the Sagaing region.

A mother and child displaced by conflict in Sagaing shelter at a monastery. (Supplied: WFP)

"The main reason the military has given for blocking this aid is they suspect these products will be used by the PDF," said Thinzar Shunlei Yi, referring to the opposition People's Defence Force.

"[The military says that] people will use it [pads] to cover their wounds."

She described the restriction as "a direct attack on women's bodies".

International humanitarian groups have also struggled to access conflict-affected regions.

"We're trying to support farming communities in Sagaing, where their livelihoods were interrupted both by the earthquake … [and] the conflict that's happening on all sides of them," said Ross Farmery, head of the International Committee of the Red Cross delegation in Mandalay.

He said landmines and unexploded ordnance were also an issue for those returning to their homes.

"They're displaced, then coming back, but there's weapons contamination," he said.

"So there's all these things on top of the earthquake."

Many buddha statues remain damaged. (AFP: Sai Aung Main)

Fragile rebuilding

About 8,300 religious monuments and temples were damaged or destroyed by the earthquake, according to UNESCO.

Among the sites damaged was the Kuthodaw Pagoda, home to a collection of Buddhist scripture tablets inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.

"When these places are harmed, communities lose anchors of memory and belonging," said a UNESCO spokesperson.

Repair of historical buildings is slow, but in cities like Mandalay, shops have reopened and on the surface, daily life appears to be resuming.

Me Nu Brick Monastery, one of the most popular tourist sites in Mandalay, was damaged by the quake. (AP: Stringer)

Even during fuel shortages, people improvise — setting up stalls beside long petrol queues to sell drinks and snacks.

But aid agencies warn the effects of the Middle East conflict on fuel, food and fertiliser are pushing more families closer to hunger.

"Disruptions to transportation, fuel rationing, and rising black-market prices are pushing up the cost of moving food," said Michael Dunford, the United Nations World Food Programme's country director in Myanmar.

"This new wave of global instability is hitting Myanmar at the worst possible moment," Mr Dunford told the ABC.

An estimated 12.4 million people — about one in four — are struggling to find enough to eat.

Fuel remains tightly controlled by the military regime.

Private cars can only operate on alternate days based on licence plates, yet shortages persist, and queues stretch for hours.

Last week, a man collapsed while waiting in the heat.

"People who survived the earthquake have barely begun to stand again, and now another blow is knocking them back down," Mr Dunford added.

People line-up for fuel for hours across Myanmar. (Reuters: Stringer)

Community support can't keep up

Many monasteries have become emergency shelters for people fleeing armed conflict near their homes and affected by the earthquake.

"Almost every monastery was already hosting displaced people," said Aye Sandar Tun, who was pregnant when the quake struck in Mandalay.

"Finding food is the main challenge for people, so even on weekends, when I am not working, I would drive around and help hard-to-reach areas," she said.

But as costs rise and donations fall, many are struggling to cope.

Quake victims run their own businesses selling food despite being homeless. (Supplied: WFP/Htet Oo Linn)

Many are trying to get by alone.

Ma Myint Myint, a street vendor, set up a samosa stall days after losing her home, but rising prices have kept her reliant on aid.

"It's a daily cycle of borrowing and scraping by," she said.

Her debts have reached 1.5 million kyats (about $1,030).

Despite this, she says others are worse off.

Ma Zin Mar Wai, a displaced mother of three, wants to return to her home in Saigaing's Wetlet township, now a conflict zone.

Displaced women from Sagaing's conflict zone set-up food stalls in Mandalay. (Supplied: WFP)

"I just want to go home," she said.

"I had a small grocery shop. I would work twice as hard — but everything has become so much more difficult.

"For now, I just hope food assistance doesn't stop.

"There are people hiding in the jungle whose situations are much worse than ours," she added.

World.title: ASX to slide as looming Iran deadline unsettles investors
World.content:
BusinessMarketsShares ASX to slide as looming Iran deadline unsettles investors STAN CHOE April 8, 2026 — 6:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Investors are nervously waiting for the latest deadline set by President Donald Trump to destroy Iran’s power plants and bridges, with futures pointing to a slight fall in the Australian sharemarket when it opens on Wednesday. The ASX futures were down slightly by 3 points, or 0.03 per cent, at 5.45am AEDT. The sharemarket closed in the green on Tuesday as oil prices moved higher. The Australian dollar has strengthened, fetching 69.67 US cents at 5.45am. Trump has threatened that a “whole civilisation will die tonight, never to be brought back again” if Iran does not meet his deadline to open the Strait of Hormuz. AP US stocks sank on Tuesday as the countdown ticked toward the latest deadline. The S&P 500 fell 0.8 per cent as Trump threatened that a “whole civilisation will die tonight, never to be brought back again” if Iran does not meet his deadline at 8pm Eastern time in the US to open the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian officials, meanwhile, urged young people to form human chains to protect sites Trump has threatened to bomb.



The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 370 points, or 0.8 per cent, with an hour remaining in trading, and the Nasdaq composite was 1 per cent lower. Related Article Opinion

Billionaires Elon Musk’s problem children could spoil his Wall Street dream Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The moves were tentative, much like they’ve been since the start of the war with Iran, because of deep uncertainty about when the fighting may end. During the first hour of Tuesday’s trading, the Dow careened between a gain of 74 points and a loss of 425. Oil prices were likewise shaky. The price for a barrel of benchmark US crude to be delivered in May briefly climbed above $US117 ($168) before settling at $US112.95, up 0.5 per cent. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, to be delivered slightly later in the year, in June, eased by 0.5 per cent to $US109.27. But it’s still well above its roughly $US70 ($100) level from before the war began in late February.



Oil prices have spiked because the war has snarled the production and transportation of crude in the Persian Gulf. Much of that oil exits the gulf through the Strait of Hormuz to reach customers around the world, but Iran has blocked it to enemies. Related Article Analysis

Middle East at war The fuel crisis is painful, but Australia has an advantage many don’t The worry in markets has been that a long-term disruption will keep oil prices high for a long time and send a painful wave of inflation crashing through the global economy. Iran on Monday rejected the latest ceasefire proposal and instead said it wants a permanent end to the war. So far in the war, Trump has made a series of threats to blow up Iranian power plants if it doesn’t open the Strait of Hormuz, only to delay it several times. The possibility remains that Trump could back down again, among other scenarios, which is keeping uncertainty high. A year ago, Trump ultimately backed off many of the stiff tariffs that he initially threatened to put on imports from other countries, though they ended up higher than from before his second term.



“Investors are likely to remain on edge and markets unable to establish trends, probably until there is a clear outcome later this evening: a deal, the US/Israeli strikes intensify, or Iran’s retaliation becomes escalatory instead of proportional,” according to Paul Christopher, head of global investment strategy at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. On Wall Street, companies with big fuel bills fell to some of the sharpest losses as high oil prices cranked up the pressure. Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings dropped 4.8 per cent, and United Airlines sank 3.6 per cent. Companies whose customers may have the least room to absorb the recent jump in gasoline prices also struggled. Dollar Tree slid 5.1 per cent, and Dollar General fell 2.3 per cent. The average price for a gallon of regular gasoline across the United States has leaped to $US4.14, according to AAA. It was below $US3 a couple days before the United States and Israel launched attacks to begin the war in late February.



In stock markets abroad, indexes fell across much of Europe. Asian stock indexes were stronger, with South Korea’s Kospi up 0.8 per cent for one of the world’s bigger gains. In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady ahead of Trump’s looming deadline. The yield on the 10-year Treasury held at 4.34 per cent, where it was late Monday. That’s well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war, and the rise has pushed up rates for mortgages and other loans going to US households and businesses, which slows the economy. World.title: ‘The most difficult’: How the Ben Roberts-Smith story was chased to ground
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Chris Masters was rattling through Afghanistan in 2008 in the back of a vehicle with special forces soldiers of Australia, notebook in hand, he had no idea the contacts he was making would lead him to the most consequential story he’d ever covered. A decade later, his journalistic collaborator, Nick McKenzie, landed in Kabul. By then, both knew their reporting could rattle Australian society and forever change the defence establishment. McKenzie was in the war-torn country on the trail of Ben Roberts-Smith. This physical giant – more than two metres tall – was Australia’s uber-soldier. With a bulging chest full of medals, he was the feature hero of the Australian War Memorial’s Afghanistan gallery. He was father of the year and allied in business to one of Australia’s richest men. Ben Roberts-Smith in Afghanistan. In 2018, Masters and McKenzie were about to allege he was also a killer multiple times over – a war criminal. “When I discussed with a senior colleague the prospect of me challenging the reputation of this eminent Victoria Cross recipient, he told me it would be like shooting Bambi,” Masters later wrote in his book, Flawed Hero.



It was, wrote McKenzie in his book, Crossing the Line, “the most difficult undertaking of my 20-year career”. Masters went to Afghanistan as Australia’s first reporter embedded with the special forces, wanting to tell how the nation’s best-trained soldiers were contributing to what was becoming this country’s longest, and ultimately most fruitless, war. Loading His stories described stunningly brave and conscientious acts of soldiery performed by the Special Air Service Regiment and the Commandos. Even as he told that story, though, Masters heard growing whispers that a small number of elite soldiers was operating without regard to the rules of armed conflict. In Kabul 10 years later, McKenzie saw the human impact. Loading



He interviewed Bibi Dhorko, the grieving wife of Afghan civilian Ali Jan – a man allegedly kicked off a cliff by Ben Roberts-Smith, then summarily executed on the same soldier’s orders. She wanted just one thing from Australia – justice for the brutal killing of her husband. For nine years, this was also the mission McKenzie and Masters took on. For years, all that was known about Ben Roberts-Smith was his legend. In his six rotations in Afghanistan, he’d become the recipient of the Victoria Cross, Australia’s highest military honour, as well as the Medal for Gallantry and a Commendation for Distinguished Service. On his return, Roberts-Smith was employed by a man who idolised him perhaps more than most – the mogul in charge of the Seven Network, the chairman of the Australian War Memorial, and a giant of Western Australia, Kerry Stokes. Stokes anointed Roberts-Smith as the executive in charge of his TV network’s Queensland division.



As the former soldier’s reputation grew, the rumours Masters had heard in Afghanistan kept niggling. So, in April 2017 he arranged to meet Roberts-Smith in Canberra to ask some questions. Editor's pick Exclusive

Roberts-Smith case The rich and influential cheer squad who backed a war criminal The retired soldier bit back. “For the first hour he reasoned, for the second hour he ranted,” Masters says. Roberts-Smith called his detractors “cowards,” “incompetent,” “toxic”. Masters, famed for his work bringing down the Queensland government in the 1980s, felt his journalistic instincts bristle. So later that year, Masters and his former protege McKenzie teamed up and got to work. As they crisscrossed Australia to test the stories they’d heard, a starkly different picture of Roberts-Smith emerged. In interviews and catch-ups with serving and former SAS soldiers in Perth, Brisbane, Canberra and Melbourne, the two reporters found many who had served alongside the big man. Some were highly decorated themselves. In even speaking, these men risked losing their jobs or facing criminal charges. But some were burning to share, mostly under a cloak of anonymity, what they claimed was an untold story that had eaten away at their consciences. Easing some of these soldiers’ minds was their long-standing relationship with Masters, forged during his trips 15 years earlier to Afghanistan. The younger McKenzie earned their trust with the intensity of his commitment and his belief in the importance of what they were doing.



As word of their investigation reached Roberts-Smith – as well as that of a parallel probe by the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force – he hit back. He called some detractors to meetings to find out what they’d said. He sent threatening letters and orchestrated a police raid on a former soldier based on false evidence. He put the word out – those speaking against him were small men jealous of his success. McKenzie and Masters were finding something quite different. They saw soldiers motivated by a desire to tell the truth to the public they’d served. Some pitied Roberts-Smith. And they believed Australia had been spun a monumental lie about the man who’d become the face of the military’s contribution to what seemed like a never-ending war. The stories from SAS soldiers built a foundation for the two reporters, but they needed corroboration. The first breakthrough came in early 2018 when the pair uncovered accounts from SAS support staff living overseas. The second breakthrough was when this masthead’s long-time Afghanistan fixer-journalist risked his life to travel to Darwan, deep in Taliban territory, to speak to key witnesses. They were 11,000 kilometres away from Australia, but they confirmed every crucial element of the cliff-kick story.

In stock markets abroad, indexes fell across much of Europe. Asian stock indexes were stronger, with South Korea’s Kospi up 0.8 per cent for one of the world’s bigger gains. In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady ahead of Trump’s looming deadline. The yield on the 10-year Treasury held at 4.34 per cent, where it was late Monday. That’s well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war, and the rise has pushed up rates for mortgages and other loans going to US households and businesses, which slows the economy.
